title: Tokens are text pieces
objectives: Explain why tokens are not necessarily whole words.
Distinguish an illustrative token split from a model-specific tokenizer.
prediction: Imagine text building blocks ['play', 'ful', ' robot', '!']. How many pieces are there, and what text do they form?
explanation: Models process text through a tokenizer, which maps text into token IDs. Tokens can correspond to a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text piece. The exact mapping depends on the model's tokenizer.

In our illustrative split, play and ful are separate pieces, while the leading space belongs to ' robot'. Four pieces reconstruct 'playful robot!'. A different real tokenizer may split that text differently.

Text length, word count, and token count are different measures. Python split() makes whitespace-separated words; it is not a universal LLM tokenizer. Even different languages and punctuation patterns can affect token counts.

Your chatbot will budget context and output in tokens. When accuracy matters, ask the configured model's token-counting interface rather than presenting a word-count guess as exact. For this lesson, our list is deliberately hand-written.
analogy_limit: Building blocks show that text can be assembled from pieces. These four pieces are illustrative and are not asserted to be Gemini's actual encoding. The code is a joiner, not a tokenizer implementation.

python_example.code:
pieces = ['play', 'ful', ' robot', '!']
text = ''.join(pieces)
print(text)
print('pieces:', len(pieces))
print('whitespace words:', len(text.split()))
walkthrough: The space before robot is inside that piece.
len(pieces) counts our manual pieces, while split() counts whitespace-separated words.
Neither measurement proves the token count for an actual hosted model.

game.title: Token Puzzle
game.instructions: Work with the manual pieces shown in each round. Do not assume these are actual model tokens. Get two of three right.

feedback.a: No piece contains a space, so none is inserted.
feedback.b: That would require adding spaces between pieces.

rounds.prompt: How many manual pieces are in ['un', 'happy', ' cat', '.']?

choices.text: Four, because the list has four items
One, because it is one sentence
Two, because there are two words

feedback.a: Word count and piece count are different.
feedback.b: Four entries form the illustrative text pieces.
feedback.c: Sentence boundaries do not determine the number of pieces.

rounds.prompt: You need the actual token count for your configured Google model. What should you do?

choices.text: Use this manual split for every model
Count spaces and call it exact
Use the model's supported counting interface

feedback.a: Space counting is an estimate of words, not exact model tokens.
feedback.b: Tokenizers vary, and our pieces were invented for teaching.
feedback.c: Use the appropriate model interface and label any fallback estimate.

questions.prompt: Must one token always equal one whole word?

choices.text: No, it may represent a smaller or different text piece
Yes, unless the code uses a dictionary

feedback.a: Tokenization is model-specific and need not match word boundaries.
feedback.c: A Python container does not determine the model's token boundaries.

questions.prompt: What is this lesson's Python code actually doing?

feedback.a: No Google SDK or tokenizer is called.
feedback.b: The pieces are already supplied, and join reconstructs the text.
feedback.c: There is no learning step or vocabulary fitting.

questions.prompt: Why do we care about tokens in a chatbot?

choices.text: They replace the need for prompts
They help measure model input/output limits and usage

feedback.b: Prompts are still input text that gets encoded.
feedback.c: Token budgets are useful for context, generation, and usage management.

build.title: Assemble a text puzzle
build.instructions: Create pieces ['chat', 'bot', ' builder', '!']. Join them, count the list entries, and count whitespace words. Add a comment saying this is a manual illustration, not a real model tokenizer.
criteria: Output includes chatbot builder!, four manual pieces, and two whitespace words.
A code comment clearly identifies the manual illustration.
hints: Use an empty string as the join separator.
len(pieces) counts pieces; len(text.split()) counts whitespace-separated words.
build.reference_solution:
# Manual illustration, not a model tokenizer.
pieces = ['chat', 'bot', ' builder', '!']
text = ''.join(pieces)
print(text)
print(len(pieces))
print(len(text.split()))

reflection: Explain why 'ten words' does not mean 'exactly ten tokens' for your chatbot.
tutor_context: Use text building blocks; clearly label all manual splits. Explain join and leading spaces. Never claim whitespace split is the actual Google tokenizer.
